extracted.intended_audience: orators, prose writers, and students of classical rhetoric
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing effective prose periods and choosing appropriate stylistic types (plain, elevated, elegant, forcible) in oratory and narrative. Covers construction of periods and members, antithesis and symmetry, metrical character (paeon), use and risks of verbal artifices, and how to order words for maximum force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form of the oratorical period
rubrics_metrics.description: The form of the oratorical period is tense and circular; it needs a neatly rounded mouth and a hand which follows closely each movement of the rhythm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose periods so they feel 'tense' from the outset (hinting they will not end simply) and circular/rounded in structure. Use tightly controlled rhythm and delivery (physical articulation) to realise the effect. Example: the quoted sentence beginning “Chiefly because I thought... I have agreed to advocate my clients’ case to the best of my ability.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Period of dialogue (lax style)
rubrics_metrics.description: The period of dialogue is lax and simpler than that of narrative; it scarcely betrays that it is a period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make dialogue-periods more relaxed: members may be flung together like disjointed style and the end may hardly reveal a formal period. The dialogue period should be midway between the resolved and the compacted style, combining features of both.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periods formed of contrasted members (antithesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Periods can be formed of contrasted members. The antithesis may lie in the thought, or it may be twofold, of thought and of expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use antithesis to create contrast either in meaning or in expression (or both). Example: “sailing across the mainland and marching across the sea.” Employ antithesis deliberately to sharpen contrast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verbally contrasted members (parallel correspondence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Members which are only verbally contrasted — article opposed to article, connective to connective, like to like, from the beginning to the end — produce a running correspondence of one thing with another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When matching words/structures across clauses (parallelism), ensure correspondence runs throughout: e.g., 'caused' to 'admired', 'coveted' to 'perilous'. This creates neat symmetry but watch for over-artifice (see risks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparent but not real antithesis (comic or mock usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some members are apparently antithetic though not really so; the turn of style counterfeiting an antithesis suggests a desire to mislead or to raise a laugh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise and use faux-antithesis for comic or mocking effect (as Epicharmus does), but be aware it imitates rhetorical artifice and can mislead or invite ridicule if used in earnest discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symmetrical members
rubrics_metrics.description: There are symmetrical members where the symmetry may be found at the beginning or at the end of the sentence; equality of members occurs when members contain an equal number of syllables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use symmetry and equal-syllable members to heighten expression and charm (examples from Panegyric, Thucydides). However, symmetry is a crafted device and must be handled carefully to avoid weakening force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homoeoteleuta (similar termination)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Homoeoteleuta’ are members which have a similar termination; they may end with the same word or the same syllable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminal similarity can add musicality but carries risk: it is ill-suited for forcible declamation because the artifice impairs force. Avoid overuse, especially in invective or passionate passages where simplicity and naturalness are needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of artifices for forceful passages
rubrics_metrics.description: Devices such as symmetry and similar termination do not contribute to force of style and are not appropriate to outbursts of passion or to delineations of character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In angry or passionate invective, prefer simple, natural, and seemingly impromptu wording. Artifices lessen vigor and may produce unintended 'mirth amid tears'. Use such devices sparingly when the aim is to excite emotion or pity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate cases for symmetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Symmetry of members can be useful in certain cases to heighten expression — removing a key word can remove the charm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply symmetry when it accentuates a point (example: parallel clauses with 'great' in both give charm; removing it reduces effect). Use deliberate symmetrical structures to amplify emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between enthymeme and period
rubrics_metrics.description: The enthymeme differs from the period: the period is a rounded structure of expression, while the enthymeme is a thought (a rhetorical syllogism) which can survive when the verbal period is broken up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use periods as forms of speech in all parts of discourse; use enthymemes as arguments (imperfect syllogisms) where reasoning is required. Do not confuse rhetorical form (period) with argumentative content (enthymeme).

rubrics_metrics.name: Member definition and period structure
rubrics_metrics.description: A member is one of the constituent parts of a period; Aristotle preferred two members though periods may be compound (three or more members).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design periods with clear members — often two — but compound periods are permissible. Be attentive to how members combine (simple or compound) to shape the overall effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four simple types of style
rubrics_metrics.description: The simple types of style are four in number: the plain, the elevated, the elegant, the forcible; there are also various combinations among them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a dominant type for a passage. The elegant may combine with plain and elevated; the forcible with both; elevated and plain stand in sharp opposition and are not readily combined. Many combinations are permissible except some oppositions (elevated vs plain).

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements of the elevated (eloquent) style
rubrics_metrics.description: Elevation consists in three things: thought, diction, and appropriate composition. The paeonic rhythm is recommended for elevation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt elevated thought and diction and compose members with paeonic character (begin with procatarctic paeon and end with catalectic paeon). Aim to begin and end members impressively (long syllables at ends).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the paeon (metrical character) in prose
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two kinds of paeon — procatarctic (initial) and catalectic (terminal). In the elevated style members should begin with a procatarctic paeon and be followed by a catalectic paeon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, structure members to start with a long syllable and end with a long syllable (paeonic character). If exact paeons are impractical, achieve paeonic effect by beginning and ending with long syllables: this creates impressiveness and elevation suitable for high style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of other metrical feet
rubrics_metrics.description: Other metrical feet have differing suitability: the heroic (spondaic) is solemn and ill-adapted for prose (clangorous), the iambic/gambic resembles ordinary talk and lacks distinction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid excessive spondaic (heroic) cadences in prose as they are too clangorous; avoid plain iambic rhythms when seeking elevation. Prefer the paeon as a mixed, safer measure for prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long members and rounded composition for grandeur
rubrics_metrics.description: Long members contribute to grandeur of style; a rounded form of composition (rounded period) secures impressiveness by limiting rests and maintaining stateliness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use longer members and rounded periods to sustain dignity and impression — do not break a stately sentence into many shorter clauses (analogy: long journeys shortened by fewer inns). Avoid sudden short members that diminish dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of harsh or clashing sounds in elevated style
rubrics_metrics.description: Words hard to pronounce in combination (clashing letters/sounds) are generally unpleasant, but in the elevated style their very excess can bring out greatness and suit the hero's depiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use harshness of sound sparingly and purposefully to convey rugged grandeur (examples from Homer and Thucydides). Recognise that smoothness and pleasant cadences are often inappropriate to elevated, rugged expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word-arrangement to augment vividness (composition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Composition (word-arrangement) augments the impressiveness of style; arranging words so that less vivid items precede more vivid ones increases force (continuous augmentation/hyperbole).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Order words and clauses to build intensity: place items of increasing vividness later to create escalation. Examples: Plato's ordering where the second verb is more striking than the first; Homer’s progressive hyperbole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-refinement in impassioned or character-drawing passages
rubrics_metrics.description: Artifice and studied devices impair the force of discourse; anger needs no art—simple and natural phrasing is the mark of passion and character-drawing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In emotional or character-focused passages, prioritize simplicity and seeming spontaneity. Avoid over-symmetry, terminal rhyme, or studied parallels that can sap emotional force or produce inappropriate amusement.
